Impact of Pre-Exercise Feeding on Substrate Utilization and Perception 
of Effort
Introduction 
Carbohydrate (CHO) quantity before exercise influences performance. 
Adequate CHO consumption prior to exercise promotes muscle and liver 
glycogen storage which may then be used for energy production during 
exercise. The International Olympic Committee on Sports Nutrition 
recommends athletes consume 5-12 grams (g) CHO per kilogram (kg) of 
body weight each day according to duration and intensity of exercise 
training. A CHO rich meal containing 140-330 g, 3-5 hours prior to exercise 
improves aerobic performance. Carbohydrate availability during exercise 
influences substrate utilization and the perception of effort during a bout 
of exercise (Melzer, 2011). Understanding how pre-exercise feeding 
affects substrate utilization and ratings of perceived exertion (RPE) 
during exercise is important for guiding pre-exercise meal decisions.  
The purpose of the study is to determine how substrate utilization and 
perceived effort during 30 minutes of vigorous exercise are impacted by 
pre-exercise feeding. It is hypothesized that a CHO rich pre-exercise meal 
will result in greater rates of CHO oxidation and lower reported RPE 
during exercise. During high intensity exercise, muscle glycogen is the 
main fuel source used for energy production (Romijn et al., 1993). For this 
reason, glycogen depletion during exercise is a limiting factor on
